title: Business strategy
overview: Business strategy is the long-term direction used to achieve corporate objectives. High-level answers must move through strategic analysis, strategic choice and implementation. The syllabus includes blue ocean strategy, scenario planning, SWOT, PEST, Porter, core competence, Ansoff, force-field analysis, decision trees, corporate planning/culture, transformational leadership, strategic change, contingency planning and crisis management.
syllabusPoints: Explain strategy and the stages of strategic management: analysis, choice and implementation.
Apply blue ocean strategy and scenario planning.
Apply SWOT, PEST, Porter's five forces, core competence, Ansoff, force-field analysis and decision trees.
Explain corporate planning/culture and transformational leadership in implementation.
Analyse strategic change, contingency planning and crisis management.

definitions.definition: A long-term direction/plan for achieving major business objectives.
A distinctive capability that creates customer value and is difficult for competitors to imitate.
Creating uncontested market space/value rather than competing head-on in an existing market.
Preparing responses to several plausible future conditions instead of relying on one forecast.
A prepared response for a foreseeable disruptive event.
A framework identifying forces driving change and forces restraining it.

sections.title: Strategic management process
content: Analysis asks where the business is now; choice compares possible strategic routes; implementation allocates people, finance, operations and controls to deliver the chosen strategy. An analytically attractive strategy can still fail if resources, culture or stakeholder support are weak.

sections.title: SWOT and PEST
content: SWOT separates internal strengths/weaknesses from external opportunities/threats. PEST scans broad external forces. Their value comes from connecting factors—for example using a strength to exploit an opportunity—not merely listing them.

sections.title: Porter's five forces and core competence
content: Five forces assess rivalry, threat of entrants/substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Strong forces tend to reduce industry attractiveness. Core competence focuses internally on hard-to-copy capabilities that create customer value, so the two frameworks answer different strategic questions.

sections.title: Ansoff matrix
content: Market penetration uses existing products/existing markets; market development existing products/new markets; product development new products/existing markets; diversification new products/new markets. Risk usually rises as the firm moves further from its existing knowledge, but actual risk depends on capability and evidence.

sections.title: Decision trees and force fields
content: Decision trees combine probabilities and financial outcomes to calculate expected values. Force-field analysis identifies drivers and restraints around change. Both structure judgement but rely on estimates and do not capture every qualitative factor.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Expected value of an outcome = probability x payoff; add weighted outcomes for each option.

sections.title: Blue ocean and scenario planning
content: Blue ocean seeks new value/market space that makes direct competition less relevant, but demand is uncertain. Scenario planning builds flexible responses to alternative futures and is valuable under uncertainty, though it is time-consuming and cannot predict every event.

sections.title: Implementation and change
content: Corporate culture may support or resist strategy. Transformational leadership can create vision and commitment. Implementation requires communication, resources, milestones and control. Contingency/crisis planning reduces reaction time when disruptions occur but plans must be updated/tested.

analysisChains.title: Market development decision
steps: The firm targets a new geographic market
Research, adaptation and distribution costs rise
Risk increases because customer behaviour is less familiar
analysisChains.evaluation: The strategy is strongest when the firm's core competence transfers well and the new market has an attractive competitive structure.

examTips: A framework is not a conclusion—use it to make and then challenge a strategic recommendation.
Paper 4 strategy answers should integrate functions: marketing choices need finance, HR capability and operational capacity.
Expected value is evidence, not automatically the best decision.
commonMistakes: Mixing SWOT internal and external factors.
Writing Ansoff definitions without applying the product/market combination.
Ignoring implementation after choosing a strategy.
Assuming diversification is always wrong because it is riskier.
